newsitem.title: USA: Simpson case jury hears pleas from both sides.
newsitem.headline: Simpson case jury hears pleas from both sides.

text.p: O.J. Simpson's lead attorney, in closing arguments on Wednesday in the ex-football star's civil trial, accused the Los Angeles Police Department and the FBI of being prejudiced against his client.
Lawyer Robert Baker said the two law-enforcement agencies had spent "thousands and thousands of their dollars ... to assist plaintiffs in a civil case," and asked, "Is that fair?"

He said the proof was that he was unable to get Los Angeles officers and detectives to testify without issuing them subpoenas, while police and agents of the Federal Bureau of Investigation freely volunteered their services to the plaintiffs.
"The FBI and the LAPD don't want a level playing field," Baker contended.

Baker's assertion added a new wrinkle to the main defence theme that Los Angeles police botched the investigation and planted evidence to frame Simpson for the June 1994 murders of his ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and her friend, Ronald Goldman.

Simpson was acquitted of double murder in October 1995 but is battling a wrongful death civil lawsuit brought by the families of the victims, who are seeking substantial damages. The civil trial was in its closing stages, with the case expected to go to the jury by late Thursday.
Baker dismissed emotional pleas from the plaintiffs' lawyers asking that his client be found responsible for the killings. "You have just been subjected to a ploy for your sympathy," he said.

Baker tried to convince the jury that Simpson could not have committed the murders at about 10:40 p.m. on the night of June 12 and still have gotten back to his mansion two miles (three km) away in time to meet a limousine driver at about 10:55 p.m.
"I'm no poet, but obviously if you don't have the time you most certainly can't commit the crime," he said.
"But I don't want this to be the mantra of this case," alluding to criminal defence attorney Johnnie Cochran's line, "If the gloves don't fit, you must acquit."
Daniel Petrocelli, who represents Goldman's father, Fred Goldman, earlier pleaded fervently with the jury to force Simpson to compensate Fred Goldman for the loss of his son.
But he stopped short of putting a figure on the amount he wants Simpson to pay, saying, "You can't put a value on the loss of a son, you can't put a price tag on it."

"True justice (for Fred Goldman) would be to see Ron Goldman walk through those doors right now, to see Nicole Brown Simpson playing with her children. That will never happen, they are gone forever," Petrocelli said.

Lowering his voice, Petrocelli, who has served as the plaintiffs' lead attorney, said there was nothing the jury could do to bring Ronald Goldman back. Then, turning and pointing his finger dramatically at Simpson, he said in a raised voice, "There is nothing he can do to bring him back."

"All you have in your power to do," Petrocelli told the panel of seven women and five men, "is to bring about some small measure of justice by requiring the man responsible to pay for Fred Goldman's loss."
But when Baker began his closing arguments, he told the jurors, "This isn't a fight for justice, it's a fight for money. It's about Mr. Simpson transferring money to Mr. Goldman."
During Petrocelli's emotionally charged second day of closing arguments, Goldman and his daughter, Kim, sobbed quietly, as did Tanya Brown, Nicole Brown Simpson's sister.
"There is no loss greater than a parent losing a child. That loss is no less if the child grows into a young man," Petrocelli said.

Petrocelli was followed to the lectern by John Kelly, the attorney for Nicole Brown Simpson's estate, who told the jury, "All we are asking you to do is assign responsibility to the man who refuses to accept it," Kelly said.
